Wall
WAWL
n. (rendering Hebrew chōmâh, qīr, and Greek teichos, mesotoichon)
From Old English weall, borrowed early from Latin vallum, a rampart or palisade — the military sense is the original one. Hebrew distinguishes what English does not: chōmâh is the city wall, the defensive circuit, while qīr is the wall of a house or a room. Almost every theologically weighted use in Scripture is the first — the wall that makes a city a city, whose breach is its ruin and whose rebuilding is its restoration.

Biblical Definition

The wall in Scripture is defence, identity, and separation together. A city without walls is the standing figure of defencelessness — he that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls. So the wall becomes the natural emblem of salvation: “We have a strong city; salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks” (Isa 26:1), where the defence is not masonry but God's own saving act. Jericho's wall is the counter-instance, where God brings down what men trusted: the people shouted, and the wall fell down flat (Jos 6:20), taken not by engineering but by obedience and a trumpet. The rebuilding of Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah is the great narrative of the theme — “come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach” (Neh 2:17) — a work of prayer, of organised labour, of a trowel in one hand and a weapon in the other, and of resisting mockery from without and discouragement from within. The New Testament then does something startling with the figure. The one wall Christ came to destroy is the wall between Jew and Gentile: He “hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us” (Eph 2:14), abolishing in His flesh the enmity, to make in Himself of twain one new man. And the last city needs no defence at all, though it has a great and high wall, because nothing that defileth shall ever enter it.

Webster 1828 Definition

The defensive circuit that makes a city a city; in Scripture the emblem of salvation appointed by God, of a ruin that shames and a rebuilding that restores, and — in its one abolished form — of the partition between Jew and Gentile broken down in the flesh of Christ.

expand to see more

WALL, n. 1. A work or structure of stone, brick or other materials, raised to some height, and intended for a defense or security.

2. The side of a building, or of a room; in the Hebrew a distinct word from the wall of a city.

3. In Scripture, a defense, protection, or means of security. Salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks. Isa. 26. They were a wall unto us both by night and by day. 1 Sam. 25.

4. To take the wall; to take the upper or inner place, as of honor or precedence in a street.

5. Middle wall of partition; the barrier between Jew and Gentile, figured by the wall in the temple beyond which no stranger might pass, and broken down in Christ. Eph. 2.

Key Scripture

Nehemiah 2:17 — "Then said I unto them, Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach."

Joshua 6:20 — "So the people shouted when the priests blew with the trumpets: and it came to pass, when the people heard the sound of the trumpet, and the people shouted with a great shout, that the wall fell down flat, so that the people went up into the city, every man straight before him, and they took the city."

Isaiah 26:1 — "In that day shall this song be sung in the land of Judah; We have a strong city; salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks."

Ephesians 2:14 — "For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us;"

Modern Corruption

Eph 2:14 is pressed into service as a general principle that all boundaries are sinful, so that the one wall Christ abolished becomes an argument for abolishing every distinction Scripture actually keeps.

expand to see more

The middle wall of partition is a specific wall: the barrier in the temple beyond which no Gentile could pass on pain of death, and behind it the ceremonial law of circumcision, meats, and days that divided Jew from Gentile. Paul says Christ abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances, to make of twain one new man. That is a defined redemptive-historical claim, and it is complete. It is not a principle that every boundary is a wall and every wall is enmity. The same apostle who wrote Eph 2 also drew hard lines — between the church and the world, between sound doctrine and corrupt, between the Lord's table and the table of devils — and the same Bible that ends the Jew-Gentile partition also ends with a city whose wall is great and high and whose gate excludes whatsoever worketh abomination.

The practical damage of the misreading is that a church which believes all walls are enmity cannot practise discipline, guard its table, or maintain an ordained ministry, because each of these draws a line. Nehemiah is the corrective narrative. The rebuilding of the wall was not xenophobia; it was the recovery of a people who had been made a reproach because they had no defined life. And the opposition Nehemiah faced — ridicule first, then threat, then the offer of a friendly meeting in the plain of Ono — is the usual sequence faced by anyone who tries to rebuild what has been broken down. His answer stands: I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew separates the city wall (chōmâh) from the house wall (qīr), and has a third word, gādēr, for the field hedge. Greek teichos is the city wall; mesotoichon, the middle wall, occurs once, in Eph 2:14.

expand to see more

Hebrew chōmâh (H2346) — a city wall, the defensive circuit; the wall of Jericho, the wall Nehemiah built, and the wall of the beloved in Son 8:9.

Hebrew qīr (H7023) — the wall of a house or chamber; the wall on which the writing appeared in Belshazzar's palace and the wall Hezekiah turned his face to in prayer.

Hebrew gādēr (H1447) — a hedge or fence about a field or vineyard; whence the hedge God set about Job, and the breaking down of the hedge in Psa 80:12.

Greek teichos (G5038) — a city wall; used of Paul let down by the wall in a basket (Act 9:25) and of the great and high wall of the new Jerusalem.

Greek mesotoichon (G3320) — a middle wall, a dividing partition; a single New Testament occurrence, Eph 2:14, and the whole doctrine of Jew-Gentile union hangs on it.

Usage

"Of defence and its loss: a city that is broken down, and without walls (Pro 25:28); they were a wall unto us both by night and by day (1Sa 25:16)."

"Of God as the true defence: salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks (Isa 26:1); I will be unto her a wall of fire round about (Zec 2:5)."

"Of the partition abolished: the middle wall of partition broken down (Eph 2:14), making of twain one new man, so making peace."
